name: binwalk
desc: Searches a binary image for embedded files and executable code
why: Carves embedded files and code out of firmware images, a classic gateway into poking at binaries and file formats.

brief.what_it_is: Binwalk is a command-line tool that scans a binary file, such as a firmware image, for other files and data embedded inside it. It can identify them and optionally extract them. The README says its main focus is firmware analysis, but it supports a wide range of file and data types. It can also run entropy analysis to help spot unknown compression or encryption. This is the v3 rewrite in Rust. The input is a binary image, and the output is a detailed list of what was found, with extracted files if requested.
brief.why_it_exists: The README presents it as an updated version of the Binwalk firmware analysis tool, rewritten in Rust "for speed and accuracy." It is meant to help people see what is packed inside a firmware blob without knowing its layout in advance.
brief.how_it_works: The README does not describe the internal mechanism in detail. It says the tool identifies embedded files and data by signature, and points to a wiki page on supported signatures. Entropy analysis, documented in a separate wiki page, is used to help identify unknown compression or encryption.

commands_seen.context: Basic usage from the README: scans the D-Link DIR-890L firmware image for embedded content and prints the results. The README says to use --help for advanced options.

brief.install_notes: The README's preferred route is a Docker image, which it says bundles all dependencies (see the wiki page on building a Docker image). Other options are installing via Cargo, the Rust package manager, or compiling from source. The README says nothing about Homebrew. Installing from the brew formula may give a different build than the Rust v3 described in the README, but I did not verify that. No hardware, accounts, or first-run configuration are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a library as well as a CLI. The README says it can be embedded in other Rust projects. It also combines signature carving with entropy graphs to flag unknown compression or encryption, which goes beyond a plain file-carving tool.
brief.status: unknown. The README describes a current v3 rewrite and links to a maintained-looking wiki, but it shows no release date, version number, or last commit. I could not check any of these from the fetched page.
brief.caveats: The README does not mention licensing, supported platforms, or known limitations. Installation requires Docker or a Rust toolchain, and the README does not describe the Homebrew build. The README is also short and points most detail to the external wiki, which I did not fetch.
quotes: This is an updated version of the Binwalk firmware analysis tool, re-written in Rust for speed and accuracy.
Usage is simple, analysis is fast, and results are detailed
Through entropy analysis, it can even help to identify unknown compression or encryption!
fetch_log: https://github.com/ReFirmLabs/binwalk: fetched OK, README returned. Not followed further; the README was enough for the brief.
